planting.note: Divide clumps or plant seed-grown plugs in spring into lean, fast-draining sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; rich, moisture-retentive soil causes weak, floppy growth.

directions: Only a named cultivar of this species was previously represented in this dataset — the plain wild species itself is a drought-tolerant clumping sedge for dune stabilization and prairie restoration, with bristly bur-like fruiting heads that add winter texture. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining sandy or gravelly soil, since richer garden beds cause the foliage to flop and weaken. It needs minimal water once established and tolerates the kind of baked, sandy slope where most ornamental sedges struggle. Divide congested clumps in spring, or start new plantings from seed on disturbed sandy ground.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into saturated, humus-rich soil along a streambank, seep, or the wet end of a rain garden; keep divisions moist until re-rooted.

directions: This large, coarse-leaved sedge holds fresh green color through summer heat better than most shade plants when kept genuinely wet, making it a strong choice for stream edges and seeps under canopy. Plant it in saturated, humus-rich soil and give it room, since it spreads gradually via short rhizomes into broad patches that look best massed. It will not tolerate the soil drying out, so reserve it for a consistently damp spot rather than an average shade bed. Divide and replant in spring, keeping new divisions evenly moist until re-established.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide rhizomatous clumps in spring and plant directly into rocky or gravelly streambank substrate subject to periodic flooding; keep moist until re-established.

directions: A true streambank specialist, this rhizomatous sedge tolerates the scouring floods and periodic submersion that would wash out most garden plants. Site it directly on a stream or pond bank in rocky or gravelly substrate rather than uniform garden soil, since it depends on the disturbance and drainage of its native habitat to perform well. Partial shade with some direct sun suits it best, and planting in groups helps stabilize eroding banks most effectively. Divide in spring and keep new plantings consistently moist until roots take hold.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and plant into consistently moist to wet soil at a pond margin, bioswale, or rain garden basin.

directions: A tough, rhizome-spreading wetland sedge widely used to stabilize saturated soil along pond edges and in floodplain restoration, this species handles brief inundation without missing a beat. Give it consistently moist to wet soil in a bioswale, rain garden basin, or pond margin, and expect it to spread by rhizome, so site it where that habit is welcome rather than in a tightly bordered bed. It tolerates full sun or light shade as long as the soil stays damp through the growing season. Cut back old foliage in late winter and divide congested stands in spring to keep spread in check.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into moist-to-seasonally-wet soil at a rain garden or pond edge; also propagated from seed for larger restoration plantings.

directions: Unlike many rhizomatous wetland sedges, this species forms a tight, non-aggressive clump, making it useful where a defined edge is wanted along a rain garden or pond border. Plant it in moist-to-seasonally-wet soil in full sun to light shade, where it tolerates brief flooding as well as short dry spells once established. It pairs well with spreading sedges that need a tidy, well-behaved neighbor to hold a bed edge. Cut back dead foliage in late winter and divide clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring, or establish from seed, into consistently moist to wet soil along a pond edge or wet meadow in full sun to part shade.

directions: Fine clumping foliage topped with distinctive pointed, bottlebrush-like seed heads gives this sedge real texture and winter interest along a pond margin or wet meadow planting. It wants consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to part shade and looks best massed in drifts rather than planted singly. In favorable wet sites it self-seeds readily, so trim spent flowering stalks if volunteer seedlings aren't wanted. Divide established clumps in spring to bulk up new plantings.

planting.note: Divide compact clumps in spring and plant into average-to-moist soil anywhere from open woodland shade to a sunnier border front.

directions: This unusually adaptable sedge tolerates everything from full sun to full shade, making it a flexible filler for the front of a mixed-light woodland bed where light conditions shift across the planting. Give it average-to-moist soil and water during establishment, after which mature clumps handle ordinary garden moisture without fuss. Its compact, non-aggressive habit and general deer resistance make it an easy companion to taller perennials and shrubs. Divide crowded clumps in spring to maintain a tidy habit.

planting.note: Divide oversized tussocks in spring and plant into consistently moist to wet soil along a streambank or the wet zone of a rain garden.

directions: A tussock-forming wet-soil sedge valued for erosion control along streambanks and rain-garden margins, this species is generally passed over by deer even in heavily browsed areas. Plant it in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to part shade, and expect it to go summer-dormant if the site dries out for an extended period. Because it forms a non-rhizomatous tussock rather than running, it stays well-behaved near a bed edge where a spreading sedge would be unwelcome. Divide oversized tussocks in spring if they outgrow their space.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
